programs.name: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for chronic pain (ACT)
founders: Steven C. Hayes (with Kirk Strosahl, Kelly Wilson)
Lance M. McCracken (pain application)
Kevin E. Vowles (pain application)
JoAnne Dahl (pain application)
Rikard Wicksell (pain application)
programs.founded_year_range: ACT origins early 1980s ('comprehensive distancing'); manual 1999; chronic-pain application 2005 (Dahl, Wilson, Luciano & Hayes, Context Press; McCracken, IASP Press); ACBS formed 2005; Stanza app (Swing Therapeutics) FDA De Novo DEN220083, 9 May 2023
programs.cost_summary: Non-proprietary model, free to use. US clinician delivery is roughly USD 100-250 per session (~USD 800-2,500 for 8-12 sessions out of pocket; typical market range, estimate), usually insurance-covered. Free at point of use in NHS pain services. Self-help books ~USD 15-25. Stanza (Swing Therapeutics) requires a prescription and is offered through clinical partners in 8 US states; no price is published (checked Swing's Stanza page and coverage news, Oct 2026). Highmark covers it for commercial members in PA, WV, DE and NY. Swing was acquired by XRHealth in July 2026.
programs.mechanism_summary: ACT attributes disability and suffering in chronic pain mainly to psychological inflexibility rather than to pain itself. The components are experiential avoidance and control efforts, cognitive fusion with pain-related thoughts, and a narrowing of behaviour away from valued activities. The theory rests on Relational Frame Theory, a behavioural account of language. ACT makes no claim that pain is brain-generated or reversible and no aetiological claims about specific syndromes. The goal is valued living with pain; pain reduction is a by-product. Mediation evidence is mixed: psychological inflexibility mediated outcomes in Wicksell 2013 and Kemani 2016, and acceptance did so in Simister 2018, but 4 of 5 path models showed no mediation in EFFIGACT (Luciano 2014).

programs.name: Alexander Technique
founders: F. Matthias Alexander (1869-1955)
Society of Teachers of the Alexander Technique (STAT, UK, 1958)
AmSAT / Alexander Technique USA (1987)
programs.founded_year_range: 1890s (Alexander developed the method for his own voice loss); taught in London from 1904; first teacher training in 1931; STAT 1958; AmSAT 1987
programs.cost_summary: Independent certified teachers (at least 1,600 h of training over 3 years, per AmSAT) set their own fees; no fee schedule is published. Sampled 2025-26 listings: US about $70-85 per 45-min lesson; UK about £40-65 per lesson. A typical course of 10-30 lessons costs roughly $700-2,500, and group courses are cheaper (e.g. a 24-week group series at $840). In trials: £596 for 24 lessons plus exercise (ATEAM, 2008 costing), and an incremental cost of £667 per patient (ATLAS).
programs.mechanism_summary: Pain and dysfunction are attributed to habitual "misuse": unconscious excess muscular effort organised around a disrupted head-neck-back "primary control." This misuse is maintained by unreliable kinaesthetic sense and by "end-gaining." Alexander treated mind and body as one psychophysical unit. Modern neuroscience reframing (Cacciatore and colleagues) presents AT as training adaptive central regulation of axial postural tone and reducing maladaptive co-contraction, with improved body awareness and self-efficacy (the latter associated with outcome in ATLAS). AT does not invoke central sensitisation, limbic, emotional or immune mechanisms. One model is applied to all complaints, and teachers do not diagnose.

founders: Dan Neuffer

programs.cost_summary: AUD 537 (approx. USD 374) for 12 months' access, per the program-details page (verified Oct 2026). Optional 1:1 coaching at AUD 139/hr, generally offered only after the course. Free intro lessons, podcast and blog.
programs.mechanism_summary: A physical plus psychological stressor (infection, vaccination, surgery, childbirth, life stress) leaves the ANS stuck in sympathetic "survival mode." Central sensitisation and a conditioned threat response keep it there. This produces secondary dysfunctions (mitochondrial, endocrine, gut, immune or infection, methylation, neurotransmitter), which in turn act as physical triggers that close a vicious loop. The Science page presents ME/CFS (including PVFS and 'adrenal fatigue'), PVFS-type long COVID, fibromyalgia, POTS, MCS, EHS and IBS as one illness. It puts SSD, FND and CRPS on the same spectrum and treats chronic Lyme and mould as secondary infections or triggers.

programs.cost_summary: 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Quiz and practitioner directory are free; Clarke's 12-chapter self-treatment course is described as free (no price on the course page). Rewiring Project membership starts at US$5.50/month (Community tier; ~$66/yr); professional tiers exist but prices are not published (checked site and archived 2025 membership page); first month free. 2026 conference registration price not posted (member discount); pre-conference workshops +$126. 2023 virtual conference was $375 with CE/CME or $275 without, 30% member discount (confirmed on Nov 2023 Wayback capture). Therapy from directory practitioners is billed separately at private rates.
programs.mechanism_summary: ATNS calls these conditions "neuroplastic symptoms." The brain has learned a danger or alarm signal and keeps firing it, producing real pain or illness with no tissue damage behind it. Stress, unrecognised emotion and trauma (especially adverse childhood experiences) set it off. Personality habits such as perfectionism, people-pleasing and self-criticism keep it going, along with fear of the symptoms. The older PPDA protocol added Sarno-style psychodynamic ideas: symptoms express intolerable emotions somatically and distract from them. ATNS rejects Sarno's oxygen-deprivation hypothesis in favour of "learned neural pathways" that can be unlearned. It uses one mechanism for every condition ("Many Symptoms, One Brain"), from back pain to ME/CFS, long COVID, chronic Lyme, MCS, POTS and EDS, with a caveat to rule out structural disease first.

programs.cost_summary: Oct 2026, USD (verified on checkout pages): Pre-Course $20 (1 month); DOC Journey course $25/mo after 14-day free trial; group coaching (Tue/Thu 12-1 pm PT Zoom) $72/mo; course+coaching bundle $87/mo; no partial refunds; flipbooks $3.99; books at retail price.
programs.mechanism_summary: Hanscom calls the core state "threat physiology": a sustained "adrenalized" fight-or-flight state caused by inescapable pain or threat, life losses and repetitive unwanted thoughts. Through neuroplasticity, chronic pain shifts to emotional circuits and becomes coupled to stress and anger. His later writing adds inflammation, glial/immune signalling, mitochondrial dysfunction and reduced prefrontal blood flow. Mental and physical pain are treated as the same phenomenon. The course FAQ states verbatim: "Almost every chronic mental and physical illness and disease arises from sustained exposure to stress chemistry." Structural lesions are the only category triaged separately, for surgical or medical care.

programs.founded_year_range: 2001-2004 (site: operating 'since 2001'; organisation co-founded 2004 per Wikipedia; charity no. 1131851; teacher training since 2010)
programs.cost_summary: Charity. programs.mechanism_summary: The core model splits primary suffering (the raw sensation of pain or illness, possibly unchangeable) from secondary suffering (resistance, aversion, catastrophising, rumination, bodily bracing, held breath, and 'blocking' or 'drowning' styles). Secondary suffering is the modifiable target. Kindly, open mindful awareness, soft breathing, compassion and pacing reduce it. The model does not claim to explain disease causes. It accepts medical diagnoses and aims to change the person's relationship to symptoms rather than cure them. One transdiagnostic model is applied to all pain, illness and stress.

programs.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Pain (CBT-CP), incl. VA national CBT-CP program
founders: Wilbert Fordyce (operant pain treatment, 1970s)
Dennis Turk, Donald Meichenbaum, Myles Genest (cognitive-behavioral pain model, 1983)

programs.founded_year_range: 1976-1983 for generic CBT for pain (Fordyce 1976; Turk, Meichenbaum & Genest 1983); VA national CBT-CP training since 2012 (patients treated from 2012, manual 2014, evaluation 2015)
programs.cost_summary: Free or copay for eligible veterans in VHA; VA manuals and workbooks are free PDFs. US private practice: many clinicians charge about USD 100-200 per session (Psychology Today), so about USD 1,200-2,400 for 12 sessions before insurance (no CBT-CP-specific price data). programs.mechanism_summary: Biopsychosocial model plus gate control/neuromatrix theory. Chronic pain is maintained by a cycle of inactivity, avoidance, deconditioning, depression and poor sleep. It is amplified by catastrophizing, low self-efficacy and operantly reinforced pain behaviours. Pain is treated as real, with nociceptive and tissue contributions, and as managed rather than cured. The goal is function and quality of life, not elimination of a brain-generated danger signal. The same transdiagnostic model is applied across pain diagnoses, with headache-specific (CBT-HA) and other condition variants.

programs.cost_summary: Free on the NHS and covered by Dutch basic insurance; private UK CBT is typically about GBP 80-150 per session, so a 12-16-session course costs roughly GBP 1,000-2,400 (USD ~1,300-3,000). programs.mechanism_summary: A trigger (usually a virus) starts the illness, and cognitive-behavioural perpetuating factors are said to maintain it. These are somatic illness attributions, fear that activity causes harm, low sense of control, focus on fatigue, avoidance or boom-bust activity patterns, physical deconditioning and sleep/circadian disruption, together forming a self-confirming vicious circle (Wessely 1989; Vercoulen 1998 Nijmegen model). GET specifically targets deconditioning and exercise intolerance. Post-exertional malaise is interpreted as deconditioning or expectation rather than a distinct physiology. The same logic is applied transdiagnostically to post-COVID fatigue and other persistent physical symptoms.

programs.mechanism_summary: The program treats these conditions as one nervous system "stuck, not broken" in a chronic stress/threat response. A trigger (infection, stress, overload) switches on an alarm that stays on. The resulting real symptoms are then read as danger, which keeps the loop going, with fear of symptoms as the key maintaining factor. A "stress threshold/bucket" (allostatic load) model has all stressors filling a single tank. Supporting language includes sympathetic overactivity, a non-resetting HPA axis, central sensitisation, vagal brain-immune signalling and neuroplastic reversibility. It is one mechanism for ME/CFS, long COVID, fibromyalgia and POTS; individualisation is through a proprietary assessment, not by disease.

programs.name: Cognitive Functional Therapy (CFT)
founders: Peter O'Sullivan (specialist musculoskeletal physiotherapist, Professor, Curtin University; director of Body Logic Physiotherapy and Evoolve)
JP Caneiro (physiotherapist, PhD, Associate Professor; co-director of Evoolve and Body Logic)
Key collaborators/co-developers (not founders): Peter Kent (Curtin; RESTORE lead; Evoolve technical support), Kieran O'Sullivan, Kjartan Vibe Fersum, Wim Dankaerts, Mary O'Keeffe, Anne Smith
programs.founded_year_range: 2006-2013 (estimate). Grew out of O'Sullivan's 2005 motor-control classification of low back pain into 'classification-based CFT'. The first RCT (Bergen, started March 2006) was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov on 20 May 2010 under the CFT name (NCT01129817). The term first appears in PubMed-indexed titles in 2013 (Vibe Fersum RCT; Caneiro case report). Definitive description in Phys Ther 2018. The Evoolve training enterprise has had an ABN since 16 Nov 2023, and the Wayback Machine first captured its site on 20 Mar 2024.
programs.cost_summary: Patients pay standard private physiotherapy fees. Body Logic does not post prices; its FAQ says its fees are higher than many practices, with 60-min initial and 30-min follow-up appointments. Typical Australian physio costs roughly AU$100-200 per session, so about 5-7 sessions comes to roughly AU$700-1,400 (about US$450-900) before rebates. The per-session figure is a general estimate, not a published survey. The Medicare chronic-disease rebate (MBS 10960) is AU$63.40 per visit, up to 5 allied-health visits a year. Clinician training through Evoolve (verified Oct 2026): the Tier 1 online course is US$330 for high-income countries, US$165 for middle-income and US$33 for low-income, plus tax, with student discounts. Masterclasses and later training tiers are priced separately. Some free courses and patient resources are offered. Evoolve describes itself as a social enterprise.
programs.mechanism_summary: CFT treats disabling low back pain as multidimensional and biopsychosocial. Pain persists through a self-reinforcing cycle with several parts: beliefs that the back is damaged or fragile; fear and catastrophising; low self-efficacy; protective movement behaviours such as bracing, breath-holding, guarded movement and avoidance; lifestyle factors such as inactivity, poor sleep and stress; and social context. Peripheral and central sensitisation are acknowledged as possible contributors, and pathology is screened for, not denied. The earlier version stressed maladaptive motor-control patterns; that rigid classification was later de-emphasised. In RESTORE, changes in self-efficacy, fear, catastrophising and early pain mediated up to about 61-62% of the treatment effect. The framework is individualised per person, not per diagnosis. It is applied mainly to musculoskeletal pain and makes no claims for ME/CFS, POTS, MCS or similar syndromes.

programs.mechanism_summary: Childhood and intergenerational trauma, defined as an internal wound that includes emotional misattunement, causes disconnection from the authentic self. programs.mechanism_summary: EAET holds that the brain generates or amplifies primary/centralized pain and other somatic symptoms. Lifetime trauma, adversity and interpersonal or intrapsychic conflict sensitize a brain "danger/alarm" system. Symptoms are expected to resolve through three processes. Patients re-attribute pain to the brain and emotion. They undergo experiential exposure to the avoided emotions, which works as a corrective emotional experience or "memory reconsolidation". They practise adaptive assertive and connecting expression in real relationships. One mechanism is applied across fibromyalgia, IBS, pelvic pain, MUS/SSD, musculoskeletal pain and headache. Patients with high trauma or conflict loads are expected to be the best candidates.

The Protectometer frames pain as the balance of 'Danger in Me' versus 'Safety in Me' cues. Reconceptualising pain (conceptual change) is the proposed active ingredient, combined with graded exposure. The scope is pain; it does not claim a single brain disorder spanning ME/CFS, MCS or POTS.

programs.mechanism_summary: The original model was 'hypothalamitis', and the program now calls it the 'Prolonged Activation State' (PAS). In this model, feelings that arise from present-day interactions are repeatedly overridden or left unanswered, and each new situation adds fresh activation. The hypothalamus, described on the site as the coordinating centre for the nervous, endocrine and immune systems, is said to stay 'on' as a result, producing fatigue, pain, brain fog, sensitivities and immune or allergy-type ('MCAS-type') symptoms. An infection can start the process, but PAS is explicitly 'not the residue of that event' and is not framed as past trauma or repressed emotion. Symptoms are treated as messages that call for a response. One model covers all of the conditions the program claims to treat.

programs.name: Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE)
founders: Eric L. Garland, PhD, LCSW (formerly University of Utah; now Endowed Professor, Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and Professor of Psychiatry, UC San Diego)
programs.founded_year_range: 2007-2008. The first pilot RCT ran in 2008 (Garland et al. 2010, J Psychoactive Drugs). The name MORE was in print by 2012, and the NASW Press manual was published in 2013.
programs.cost_summary: Patients: no published price. MORE is billed as group/individual psychotherapy or group medical visits where offered (e.g. Essentia Health since 2021), and is free in trials. Clinicians: online certification course lists at USD 895, on sale at USD 716 (institute.moretherapy.com, Oct 2026). It is a one-time payment for annual membership and includes 12 self-paced modules (~10 h), monthly live sessions, a free annual subscription to the companion app and up to 10 CE hours (NAADAC/NASW-Utah). Earlier 2-day live trainings cost USD 500. Guilford manual published 2024.
programs.mechanism_summary: MORE uses a "downward spiral" allostatic model in which chronic pain, negative affect and opioid use reinforce one another. Opioid exposure produces hedonic dysregulation: drug cues gain salience (attentional bias, cue-reactivity, craving) while natural rewards lose value (anhedonia). This combines with attentional bias toward pain and catastrophizing appraisals. Treatment targets the attention–appraisal–reward interface with three skills. Mindfulness reinterprets pain as neutral sensations and interrupts automatic habits. Reappraisal reduces catastrophizing. Savoring restores natural-reward responsiveness. Proposed biomarkers include HRV during meditation (Am Psychol 2020), frontal-midline theta (Neuropsychopharmacology 2021) and LPP/P300 reward responses (Sci Adv 2019). The model stays within mainstream neuroscience and is used alongside medication; it does not claim pain is purely brain-generated.

Research protocols for fibromyalgia target amygdala/limbic or pgACC-S1 networks (central sensitisation). NeurOptimal rejects diagnosis-specific protocols: it interrupts music at EEG 'turbulence' so the brain 'self-organises'. Muse trains meditation attention. Fibromyalgia, IBS, ME/CFS, migraine and chronic pain are seen as overlapping "functional disorders," possibly "ONE condition with different aspects." Core FND symptoms are distinguished from these associated ones, and comorbid organic disease is acknowledged.

calibration_notes: Harmonized from all 74 entries in popularity_raw.json; no web lookups were made. ENGAGED = cumulative people who actually enrolled in, were treated with, bought, or meaningfully used the program at least once. Book PURCHASERS count; readers of borrowed copies do not. Registered or active app users count, but not raw downloads. AUDIENCE = cumulative unique people exposed: followers, unique viewers (YouTube views divided by about 10-30 to get unique viewers), podcast listeners, site visitors and press, and it is always >= engaged. Calibration: (1) hard numbers were taken at face value. Examples: ENO Breathe 4,829 completers, Nerva's 195k real-world dataset, NeuroStar >250k patients, Tapping Solution 868k unique users, Dispenza's 22k retreat roster, Coursera 9.8k, VA CBT-CP >=14k. (2) Unaudited company 'helped/served' claims were discounted 0.2-0.5 log10. Examples: Gupta 40k to 10^4.4, Lightning Process 75k to 10^4.6, Curable 1M+ to 10^5.6, CMBM Gaza/Haiti, Breathworks 100k. (3) Researcher reach values that were really audience were moved to audience_log10, with engaged set much lower: YouTube-led programs such as Raelan Agle, Pain Free You, CFS Health and Irene Lyon, plus Compassionate Inquiry, which uses Mate's film/book audience, and neurosymptoms.org, which uses site visits. (4) Umbrella practices count only health, clinical or self-care use relevant to chronic conditions, globally. Yoga therapy covers therapeutic or condition-specific yoga only, with general yoga (>10^8) excluded. Tai chi/qigong covers health-motivated and structured health programs only, with recreational/martial practice in China excluded. EMDR, IFS, SE, polyvagal, TMS and neurofeedback count clinical or self-care use for any chronic mental or physical condition, not pain only; pain-specific subsets are 1.5-2 log units smaller (for example, EMDR for pain is about 10^4.5). CBT and ACT count pain-specific delivery only. Interdisciplinary pain rehab counts the generic global model, of which Mayo alone is about 10^4.4. Rank check: meditation apps (7.9) > yoga therapy / tai chi (7.0-7.1) > EMDR / Relaxation Response / EFT / Wim Hof / MBSR / IFS / Dispenza / Sarno (6.1-6.6) > MBCT / PNE / CBT-CP / interdisciplinary rehab (6.0-6.2) > Curable / nVNS / Nerva / PRT (5.2-5.7) > DNRS / Gupta / LP (4.4-4.6) > small brain-retraining businesses (3.2-4.0) > PSRT (2.0). Trajectories are the researcher relative-activity curves read as relative new engaged users per year, mostly unchanged. Changes: pre-1960 total entries were added at year 1959 for Alexander (40) and Feldenkrais (6), and the CBT/GET 2011 PACE media spike was smoothed. Some curves start before the founding year, where predecessors existed (for example, the Relaxation Response from 1970). Confidence is low for most entries because the numbers are Fermi estimates. It is high only where a hard count exists (ENO Breathe, Nerva, PSRT). HARMONIZED SCALES. engaged_log10 = cumulative people who enrolled in, were treated with, or meaningfully used the program at least once (book PURCHASERS count; free-content viewers do not). audience_log10 = cumulative unique people exposed (viewers, readers, listeners, site visitors), always >= engaged. Researcher reach_log10 values mixed these two definitions, so each program was re-derived.

CONVERSION RATIOS (applied explicitly; see each basis):
(1) YouTube: unique viewers = total views / 10 (/12 for long-running channels; /25 for daily-upload channels such as Pain Free You). Subscribers are about 5-10% of uniques. Creator-led paid programs convert ~1-3% of unique viewers to engaged users. A single YouTuber's views are counted as audience only.
(2) Apps: unique users = downloads x ~0.5-0.6 after repeat-install and cross-app overlap. Meaningful use (≥1 session) = ~50-65% of registered users; company 'users' or signup claims are discounted ~0.25-0.65. Rating counts are a cross-check, at roughly 1 rating per 10-15 active users (calibrated on Nerva: 32.5k iOS ratings, 3x10^5 users).
(3) Trustpilot: ~30 customers per review (calibrated on Lin Health: 613 reviews, ~2x10^4 patients).
(4) Podcasts: regular listeners = cumulative downloads / ~150.
(5) Websites: uniques = visits / ~8; ~15% use the site as structured self-help.
(6) Clinician-delivered methods: trained clinicians actually practising x clients per career (10-50 depending on intensity).
(7) Books: copies sold x ~0.8 = unique purchasers.
(8) Vendor 'reached/helped' claims are discounted 20-50% unless corroborated.

UMBRELLA PRACTICES. Yoga therapy, tai chi/qigong, EMDR, CBT for pain, neurofeedback, PNE/Explain Pain, interdisciplinary pain rehab and rTMS count only health, clinical or self-care use relevant to chronic conditions, globally. General fitness yoga (>10^8) and general Chinese park tai chi are excluded. EMDR counts all clinical (trauma/PTSD) use; pain-specific EMDR is ~10^4.5. Meditation apps, Wim Hof, nVNS consumer devices and Muse are counted as self-care use, with no pain-only restriction (noted in basis).

WEB LOOKUPS (6): Joe Dispenza YouTube ~1.74M subs (socialcounts/sponsorradar/creatordb, mid-2026); Wim Hof iOS app ~1.7M installs, ~110k MAU (AppGoblin, May 2026) plus developer claim of >1M downloads per store; Tapping Solution Android 1M+ installs, 22k US iOS ratings. Searches for subreddit sizes (r/TMSTherapy, DNRS) returned no usable counts, so subreddit and Google Trends signals were not quantified. Ranks rest on YouTube, app, Trustpilot, forum and book-sales signals instead.

SANITY ORDER CHECK: meditation apps (7.9) >> yoga therapy (7.2) > tai chi (6.9) > Wim Hof (6.6) > MBSR (6.3) ~ IFS > Sarno (6.1) > Curable (5.4) > PRT (5.2) > DNRS = Gupta (4.7) > YouTube-led programs such as Raelan Agle and CFS Health (3.9 engaged, but 5.6-6.0 audience) > re-origin (3.2) > PSRT (2.0).

TRAJECTORIES. These are researcher relative-activity points re-used as relative new engaged users per year (any scale), checked against indicators: launch years, app-store dates, the 2020-22 pandemic spike for apps and online programs, the 2021 PRT/JAMA spike, the 2017 Sarno documentary and the 2021 NICE GET reversal. Pre-1960 activity is collapsed into one 1959 entry for Alexander Technique (15) and Feldenkrais (5). For umbrella practices (yoga, tai chi), points before the named program's founding are kept because the umbrella count includes them.

Main uncertainties: book-sales figures are mostly unaudited; umbrella restriction shares are judgment calls (±0.4 log); vendor claims for small brain-retraining programs are ±0.3 log.

engaged_log10 = cumulative people who enrolled in, were treated by or meaningfully used the program. That covers course or app users with at least one real session, therapy/class clients, device buyers, and book purchasers for book-based methods. audience_log10 = people exposed: YouTube and podcast viewers (views converted to unique people at roughly 10-25 views per person), site visitors, media and social reach. audience is never below engaged.

How the estimates were made: they are anchored first on institutional reach, i.e. certified practitioners x plausible caseload, clinics and hospitals, guideline adoption (NICE, VA, CDC), insurance or payer coverage, and national rollouts (NHS PMPs, VA CBT-CP, German multimodal pain therapy, Danish regional units). Vendor claims come next and are discounted about 0.1-0.3 log when unaudited. A single influencer's view count is never counted as engagement, so Raelan Agle, Dan Buglio, CFS Health, Irene Lyon and Optimum Health have wide engaged-audience gaps.

Umbrella practices (yoga therapy, tai chi/qigong, EMDR, CBT for pain, neurofeedback/biofeedback, TMS, interdisciplinary rehab, PNE, IFS, SE, polyvagal) count only use for health, clinical or self-care purposes relevant to chronic conditions, globally. Recreational fitness yoga, martial tai chi and general psychotherapy uses are excluded. EMDR and TMS include PTSD and depression treatment, since these are chronic conditions; pain-specific EMDR alone would be ~10^4.5.

Resulting rank order: meditation apps (8.0) > tai chi/qigong (7.4) ≈ yoga therapy (7.2) > EMDR, PNE, relaxation response, MBSR, CBT for pain, interdisciplinary rehab (6.3-6.6) > Sarno, IFS, Dispenza, EFT, Wim Hof (6.1-6.3) > ... > DNRS/Gupta (~4.6) > small limbic-retraining courses (3.4-3.9) > PSRT (2.0).

Trajectories are the researcher's relative-activity anchor points, kept mostly as given, rescaled as relative new engaged users per year. Interpolate linearly between the anchor years; the scale is arbitrary within each program. The only additions are pre-1960 total entries, stored as year 1959 (Alexander technique 60, Feldenkrais 5), and 1960 start points for tai chi and yoga therapy.

Web lookups were limited to 3: Nerivio (~35k US users by 2022), tai chi NHIS prevalence (1.2-1.7% of US adults, 2007-2017) and German OPS 8-918 volumes (no national total found).
